strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem setup: neural combinatorial optimization on multigraphs and asymmetric graphs with multiple conflicting objectives, which has been largely overlooked in the existing NCO literature.

Proposes two distinct, well-reasoned architectures: GMS-EB (a direct autoregressive edge-based solver) and GMS-DH (a scalable two-stage approach that prunes parallel edges before routing), accompanied by an effective multi-sample RL formulation for bilevel training.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation covering multiple problem variants (MOTSP, MOCVRP, MGMOTSP, MGMOTSPTW), comparing against diverse baselines including classical solvers (LKH-3, OR-Tools), multiple MOEAs, and competitive neural baselines.
Good generalization performance demonstrated in zero-shot transfer across larger problem sizes (up to 200 nodes) and larger numbers of parallel edges (up to 10 edges per node pair).
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: the core components are largely assembled from existing techniques, combining the GREAT encoder, Pointerformer/Multi-Pointer decoder, POMO multi-start training, and hypernetwork-based scalarization.

High computational and training overhead: GMS-EB requires significant training time (1.7 hours per epoch on 50 nodes) and its augmented inference is slower than LKH3 on 100-node instances (Table 1), while GMS-DH trades off some solution quality to maintain tractability.

Independence assumption in GMS-DH pruning: selecting edges independently for each node pair a priori restricts the model from capturing route-dependent or time-dependent edge feasibility, which is especially relevant in constrained settings like time windows.

Lack of real-world benchmarks: despite motivating multigraph routing with practical applications such as road networks and logistics, experiments are exclusively conducted on synthetic distributions (TMAT, XASY, FLEX, FIX).

strengths: Pioneering formulation for neural combinatorial optimization: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to address multi-objective routing directly on multigraphs using learning-based methods, expanding neural solvers beyond standard simple/Euclidean graphs.

Well-motivated dual-architecture approach: The paper introduces both an edge-autoregressive solver (GMS-EB) and a scalable two-stage dual-head model (GMS-DH) that decouples parallel edge pruning from route construction. The reinforcement learning training algorithm for the dual head (using sampled rollouts from the routing decoder as feedback for the selection head) is clean, principled, and effective.

Comprehensive experimental validation: The authors evaluate across several multi-objective problems (MOTSP, MOCVRP, MGMOTSP, and MGMOTSPTW) and diverse graph topologies (Euclidean, asymmetric TMAT, and highly asymmetric XASY). The method demonstrates strong performance against classical heuristics (LKH, OR-Tools), multiple multi-objective evolutionary algorithms, and neural baselines.

Solid ablations and generalization studies: The paper provides insightful analyses showing the necessity of learned pruning on non-linear/complex problems (MGMOTSPTW) compared to naive pre-pruning heuristics, along with convincing zero-shot generalization experiments up to 200 nodes and 10 parallel edges.
weaknesses: High computational cost and scaling bottleneck of GMS-EB: GMS-EB scales as O(M N^4) when coupled with POMO rollouts, resulting in heavy per-epoch training times (1.7 hours for N=50) and requiring curriculum fine-tuning shortcuts for N=100.

Absence of specialized OR heuristics for multigraphs with time windows: For MGMOTSPTW, the comparisons are restricted to MOEAs and 'implicit' LKH/OR-Tools (which ignore time windows in the objective during search). Benchmarking against established operations research metaheuristics for multigraph routing (such as multigraph ALNS) would provide a stronger point of reference.

Evaluation limited to synthetic distributions: While the synthetic FLEX and FIX distributions provide controlled benchmarks, evaluating on real-world multimodal transport networks or road multigraph datasets (e.g., with realistic travel time vs. toll vs. distance trade-offs) would further strengthen the practical claims.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem in Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO): multi-objective routing on multigraphs and asymmetric graphs, which is well-motivated by realistic transport network scenarios.

Proposes two distinct and sensible paradigms: a direct edge-based autoregressive construction model (GMS-EB) and a decoupled two-stage prune-then-route architecture (GMS-DH) to balance computational complexity and solution flexibility.

Provides an extensive empirical evaluation covering multiple problem variants (MOTSP, MOCVRP, MGMOTSP, MGMOTSPTW), different cost distributions (TMAT, XASY, FLEX, FIX), and comparisons against MOEAs, scalarized classical heuristics (LKH3, OR-Tools), and neural baselines.
The manuscript is clearly structured, with comprehensive supplementary material detailing architectures, training procedures, and extensive zero-shot / out-of-distribution analyses.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: The core components are largely assembled from existing literature (GREAT edge encoder, Multi-Pointer decoder, hypernetwork-based preference conditioning from COSMO/Pareto-set learning, and POMO multi-start training).

Conceptual limitation of the GMS-DH model: In GMS-DH, the edge-pruning decision is made globally and statically prior to the tour rollout. For problems with dynamic state variables such as MGMOTSPTW (where arrival time at a node strictly determines which edge between two locations is optimal), decoupling edge selection from the current rollout state is conceptually suboptimal.

Lack of realistic or real-world multigraph benchmarks: Despite emphasizing real-world supply chain and transport network motivation (e.g., citing Ben Ticha et al.), all multigraph evaluations rely entirely on synthetic random uniform distributions (FLEX and FIX). Testing on realistic road network topologies or established VRPTW multigraph instances would significantly strengthen the empirical claims.

Weak baselines on constrained multigraph problems: For the MGMOTSPTW experiments, the paper benchmarks against 'implicit' LKH and OR-Tools heuristics that ignore time windows entirely, rather than comparing against dedicated multigraph metaheuristics (such as ALNS or tabu search variants designed for multigraph routing).

High computational cost and poor scaling of GMS-EB: As an edge-based model with POMO rollouts, GMS-EB exhibits an O(M N^4) complexity, resulting in heavy training times (1.7 hours per epoch on instances of only 50 nodes), making it challenging to scale to realistic problem sizes without severe downsampling.

strengths: Novel and practically relevant problem setting: While neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) has primarily focused on simple graphs (predominantly Euclidean coordinate-based), routing over multigraphs is common in real-world transportation networks (e.g., alternative routes with distinct travel times and costs). This paper provides the first neural routing framework specifically addressing multigraphs.

Well-motivated dual architecture design: The paper proposes two complementary models—GMS-EB (an edge-based autoregressive model) and GMS-DH (a dual-head model combining non-autoregressive learned edge pruning with autoregressive node routing). GMS-DH effectively reduces the decoding complexity from O(MN^4) to O(N^3).

Principled training formulation: The collaborative reinforcement learning formulation for GMS-DH (training the pruning head using the maximum reward achieved across sampled tours from the routing head, alongside a shared encoder) is sound and novel in this context.

Extensive empirical evaluation: The authors benchmark across multiple problem variants (MOTSP, MOCVRP, MGMOTSP, MGMOCVRP, and MGMOTSP with time windows), diverse graph distributions (TMAT, XASY, FLEX, FIX), varying instance sizes (up to 200 nodes and 10 parallel edges), and tri-objective settings. Comparisons against strong classical solvers (LKH3, HGS, OR-Tools), genetic algorithms, and adapted neural baselines (MBM, GOBM, GRBM) are thorough.

Insightful ablations: The comparison with heuristic pruning (GMS-DH Simple) and pre-encoder pruning (GMS-DH PP) clearly demonstrates the benefits of learning edge selection post-encoding, particularly on problems like MGMOTSPTW where simple a priori edge elimination is not viable.
weaknesses: Training computational overhead: Training GMS-EB is relatively expensive (e.g., 1.7 hours per epoch on 50-node multigraphs), necessitating curriculum learning. While GMS-DH partially mitigates this, training times remain substantially higher than simple graph baselines like MBM.

Lack of real-world road multigraph evaluations: The experiments rely entirely on synthetic benchmark distributions (FLEX, FIX, TMAT, XASY). Evaluating on real road networks (e.g., derived from OpenStreetMap or benchmark instances from the operations research literature, such as Ben Ticha et al.) would have provided stronger validation of real-world applicability.

Limited competitive margin on linear MOTSP: On simpler problems where Proposition 1 holds and linear scalarization allows exact pre-pruning, pre-pruned baselines (like MBM) remain competitive and faster to train, making the primary advantage of GMS most apparent on complex constraints like time windows.

strengths: Tackles an important and under-explored problem in Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO): extending neural solvers beyond simple Euclidean graphs to multigraphs and asymmetric graphs, which are prevalent in real-world routing scenarios.

Proposes two distinct and sensible architectures: GMS-EB (direct edge-level autoregressive decoding) and GMS-DH (a two-stage hybrid framework combining non-autoregressive parallel edge pruning with autoregressive tour construction) to balance solution quality and computational scalability.

The collaborative reinforcement learning formulation for GMS-DH is well-designed, effectively bypassing the lack of ground-truth optimal edge-pruning labels by using routing rollouts to supervise the selection head.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple problem classes (MOTSP, MOCVRP, MGMOTSP, MGMOCVRP, and MGMOTSPTW), comparing against strong OR solvers (LKH-3, HGS, OR-Tools), multi-objective evolutionary algorithms (MOEAs), and adapted neural baselines, backed by solid zero-shot generalization and tri-objective results.
weaknesses: Limited evaluation on real-world routing topologies: The paper heavily motivates multigraphs through realistic road networks (e.g., trade-offs between tolls, distance, and transit time), yet the experiments rely exclusively on synthetic random distributions (FLEX, FIX, TMAT, XASY) rather than real road network benchmarks (e.g., OpenStreetMap-derived multigraphs or established OR benchmarks from Ben Ticha et al.).

Architectural novelty is largely a synthesis of existing techniques: The individual components (GREAT encoder, Multi-Pointer decoder, hyper-network conditioning from Lin et al., and POMO RL training) are adapted from prior works, making the core technical novelty relatively modest.

Training efficiency and stability challenges: GMS-EB suffers from high decoding complexity ($O(MN^4)$), leading to prohibitive training times on larger graphs. While GMS-DH improves scalability, its multi-head RL training requires careful heuristic scaffolding (curriculum learning across graph sizes, pre-training the routing decoder on simple graphs, and freezing encoder gradients for the selection head) to remain stable.

In several benchmark settings, highly optimized classical heuristics (such as LKH-3 and HGS) still maintain an advantage in hypervolume, showing that the neural methods primarily compete on inference speed rather than raw solution quality.

strengths: Novel and practically relevant problem setting: While the neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) literature has almost exclusively concentrated on simple (mostly Euclidean) graphs, multigraph representations are widespread in practical transport networks where competing trade-offs (e.g., distance, transit time, toll costs) exist between node pairs.

Well-motivated dual-architecture design: The paper provides two distinct paradigms to address the complexity trade-off in multigraph routing: GMS-EB (direct autoregressive edge selection, high accuracy but O(M N^4) roll-out complexity) and GMS-DH (a two-stage approach leveraging non-autoregressive parallel edge pruning followed by node-based autoregressive routing, achieving O(N^3) complexity).

Extensive empirical benchmarking: The authors evaluate multiple problems (MOTSP, MOCVRP, MGMOTSP, MGMOCVRP, and MGMOTSPTW), multiple graph distributions (TMAT, XASY, FLEX, FIX), tri-objective formulations, and zero-shot scaling up to 200 nodes. Comparisons include multiple MOEAs, single-objective heuristics under scalarization (LKH3, HGS, OR-Tools), and adapted neural baselines (MBM, GRBM, GOBM).

Insightful ablations: The ablation study comparing learned pruning vs. heuristic pre-pruning (and the challenging MGMOTSPTW setting where simple linear pruning fails) clearly justifies the necessity of the proposed learned selection mechanism.
weaknesses: Lack of real-world network benchmarks: The motivation heavily emphasizes the real-world significance of multigraph routing over road networks (referencing Ben Ticha et al. and Lai et al.), yet all evaluations are conducted on synthetic, randomly generated instances (FLEX and FIX). Validating the methods on real-world road multigraph datasets (e.g., OpenStreetMap-derived multigraphs with actual travel times and distances) would significantly strengthen the empirical claims.

High training cost and optimization complexity: As reported in Appendix D, training GMS-EB is computationally heavy (1.7 hours per epoch on 50 nodes for multigraphs, totaling hundreds of GPU hours). Furthermore, GMS-DH requires intricate curriculum learning, freezing encoder gradients for the selection decoder, and pre-training on simple graphs to prevent policy collapse.

Limited architectural novelty of core components: The individual building blocks are largely adapted from prior work: the GREAT encoder from Lischka et al. (2025), the Multi-Pointer decoder from Jin et al. (2023), preference hypernetworks from Navon et al. (2021) / Lin et al. (2022), and POMO reinforcement learning from Kwon et al. (2020). The primary technical contribution lies in the system-level orchestration and dual-stage formulation rather than novel neural primitives.

Problem scale remains modest: Main training and evaluations are restricted to N <= 100, with zero-shot testing up to N = 200. In practical multigraph logistics, networks typically involve many hundreds or thousands of nodes, and it remains unclear how well GMS-DH's independent edge-filtering assumption holds as scale expands substantially.
